title: Local SEO and Google AI Overviews: What to Fix First
dek: Local SEO when Google answers with AI first: where AI Overviews get local business facts, how local ranking works, and the fixes that matter most.
keywords: how to show up in AI Overviews locally
summary: Local SEO still works when Google answers with AI first, and the core work barely changes. Google says AI Overviews and AI Mode need no special optimization. They draw on your Google Business Profile, your website and your reviews, so an accurate profile, plain service pages and steady reviews are what get a local business named.

hero.alt: Momo the blue robot mascot as a noir beat cop studying a city street map under a lamppost with a magnifying glass, in dramatic ink and halftone on cream newsprint

takeaways: Google says there are no extra requirements to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode, so standard local SEO is still the job.
Your Google Business Profile feeds both the map pack and Google's AI answers, which makes it the first thing to fix.
Local results still depend mainly on relevance, distance and prominence, and Google says you cannot pay for a better local ranking.
Reviews and matching facts across your profile and website give an AI summary something accurate to say about you.
Search Console's generative AI performance report shows how often your pages appear in AI Overviews and AI Mode.

body.heading: What changes on a local search page with AI Overviews?
paragraphs: A local search on Google can now open with an AI Overview, a short written answer that sits above the map pack and the regular links. Ask for an emergency plumber or a brunch spot nearby, and the summary may name businesses, mention hours or compare a few options before anyone scrolls.
The map pack and the organic results are still on the page. What changed is the reading order, which now puts the summary first and your listing second.

Google also offers AI Mode, a conversational search that can handle longer local questions like which roofer near me handles insurance claims. Both features run on the same index and the same business data, so the work in this guide covers both.
For a customer, this saves a step. For a business, it means the facts Google holds about you get read first, before your own listing gets a look.

body.heading: Do you need special optimization to show up in AI Overviews?
paragraphs: No, Google says you do not. Its [AI features documentation on Google Search Central](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ai-features) states there are no additional requirements to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode and no special optimizations needed beyond normal SEO best practices.

Google's [guide to optimizing for generative AI features](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/ai-optimization-guide) adds one point that matters a lot for local businesses. It says an accurate Google Business Profile can help your business show up in both AI responses and regular search results.

That is good news for a small business with a small budget. There is no separate local AI tool to buy and no secret file to add, which is the same idea behind [generative engine optimization](/daily/what-is-generative-engine-optimization). The difference now is that gaps in your basics show up in the very first thing a customer reads.

If someone pitches you an AI SEO package for local search, ask what it changes on your profile, your website and your reviews. If the answer is none of those, it is probably not touching what Google reads.

body.heading: Where does Google get local business information for AI answers?
paragraphs: Google pulls from the same places it uses for the rest of local search: your Google Business Profile, your website and what the rest of the web says about you. No hidden source exists, so the fastest way to change what the summary says is to fix those three.

subsections.heading: Your Google Business Profile
paragraphs: Your Business Profile is the most structured record Google has about you. Name, primary category, hours, service area, phone number and description all feed the map pack directly.
When those fields are wrong or empty, an AI summary has less to work with or, worse, repeats the wrong detail.

subsections.heading: Your website
paragraphs: Your website confirms and expands what the profile says. A service page that names the town, the service and the hours in plain words gives Google text it can match to a real question.
Pages built this way are also the ones [answer engines quote](/daily/write-pages-answer-engines-quote), because the answer sits in the first sentence instead of under a slogan.

subsections.heading: Reviews and mentions elsewhere
paragraphs: Reviews and outside mentions tell Google how known and trusted you are. Google's own help page says review count, review score and links from other websites all feed into local ranking.
Specific recent reviews also give a summary real detail to repeat, like on time, fair quote, cleaned up after.

body.heading: How does Google decide which local businesses to show?
paragraphs: Google says local results are based mainly on relevance, distance and prominence, and AI features did not change that. Its [local ranking tips for Google Business Profile](https://support.google.com/business/answer/7091) also say there is no way to request or pay for a better local ranking.

subsections.heading: Relevance
paragraphs: Relevance is how well your profile matches what someone searched for. Complete, detailed business information helps Google match you to more of the right searches.

subsections.heading: Distance
paragraphs: Distance is how far your business is from the person searching or the place they named. You cannot change your address, but you can make sure your service area is listed correctly.

subsections.heading: Prominence
paragraphs: Prominence is how well known your business is, online and off. Google says links from other sites, review count and review score all count toward it, and your position in regular web results counts too.
Prominence is also where AI answers and the map pack overlap most. The same reviews and mentions that lift you in the map give a summary real detail to repeat.

body.heading: What should a local business fix first?
paragraphs: Fix your Google Business Profile first, because it feeds both the map pack and the AI summary. Then work outward to your website and your reviews in this order.

Step 1: Open your Business Profile and check every field. Confirm the business name, primary category, hours, holiday hours, service area, phone number and website link, then write a description that says what you do, for whom and where.

Step 2: Make your website match the profile word for word on the basics. Your homepage and each service page should name the town or service area, the service and how to reach you in plain sentences, not only in a logo or footer.

Step 3: Give each main service its own page. A page that answers the top three questions customers ask about that service gives Google and AI answers a clear source, and [schema markup](/daily/schema-markup-for-ai-answers) can label the business facts on it.
Step 4: Ask every happy customer for a review and reply to every review you get. A calm, specific reply to a bad review shows future customers you are paying attention.
Step 5: Add real photos of your work, your team and your storefront. Photos help customers know what to expect before they call, and they round out a complete profile.

Step 6: Check your results once a month. Search Console's [generative AI performance report](https://support.google.com/webmasters/answer/16984139) shows impressions from AI Overviews and AI Mode by page, country and device, and our guide to [measuring AI search visibility](/daily/measure-ai-search-visibility) covers the rest.

body.heading: A simple worked example: two plumbers in one town
paragraphs: Here is an example with made-up numbers, not a statistic. Plumber A and Plumber B both serve the same town, and both get about 40 calls a month from Google.

Plumber A lists six services on its Business Profile, but its website only mentions two of them. If 1 in 4 calls is about water heaters, that is 10 calls a month tied to a service the website barely mentions, so an AI summary has little to say about Plumber A for that question.

Plumber A adds a water heater page and asks its last 30 customers for a review. If 1 in 3 of them leaves one, that is 10 new reviews, moving the profile from 18 reviews to 28 and giving Google fresh, specific detail to work with.
Nothing about this required a new tool. It took one page, one profile check and one round of review requests, which is the kind of work a small team can finish in a week.

body.heading: What are the most common local SEO mistakes with AI search?
paragraphs: The most common mistake is treating AI search as a separate project and letting the basics slide. These are the others that show up again and again.

subsections.heading: Hours that are wrong on holidays
paragraphs: Holiday hours are the detail most often left out of date. A customer who reads an AI summary saying you are open, then finds a locked door, does not come back. Set a reminder two weeks before each holiday to update them.

subsections.heading: A website that never says where you work
paragraphs: Many small business sites mention the town only in the footer or not at all. If the page does not say it in a sentence, Google has to guess.

subsections.heading: Chasing tricks instead of facts
paragraphs: Google's guide lists things it says are not needed for its AI features, including llms.txt files and special markup made just for AI. Time spent on tricks is time not spent on the profile and pages that actually feed the answer.

subsections.heading: Different facts in different places
paragraphs: When your profile, website and directory listings disagree on hours or phone number, Google has to pick one. Choose one version of every basic fact and use it everywhere.

subsections.heading: Ignoring reviews
paragraphs: A profile with a handful of old reviews gives Google little to go on. A steady habit of asking for reviews matters more than a one-time push.

body.heading: When is extra work on AI Overviews worth it?
paragraphs: For most local businesses, the extra work is simply doing the basics well and checking them monthly. Whether to go further depends on how your customers search.

subsections.heading: It makes sense if
paragraphs: Your customers ask longer questions before they call, like which dentist near me takes my insurance or which contractor handles permits. It also makes sense if competitors keep showing up in AI summaries for services you offer, which you can confirm by [checking how AI answer engines cite businesses](/daily/get-cited-by-ai-answer-engines) in your area.

It also makes sense when one of your services is worth far more than the rest, like implants for a dentist. A page that answers that service's questions in depth gives AI answers a clear source for exactly that job.

subsections.heading: You can keep it simple if
paragraphs: Most of your business comes from repeat customers, referrals or one or two short searches like your business name. In that case, an accurate profile, a clear website and a monthly review check cover almost everything.

faq.question: Can a small local business show up in a Google AI Overview?
faq.answer: Yes. Google uses the same index and business data for AI Overviews as for its regular results, so a complete profile, a clear website and real reviews give a business of any size a fair shot.

faq.question: Can I pay Google to rank higher in local results or AI answers?
faq.answer: No. Google says there is no way to request or pay for a better local ranking, and its AI features draw on the same ranking systems as regular search.

faq.question: Do I need an llms.txt file for local AI search?
faq.answer: No. Google's guide to its generative AI features says llms.txt files and special AI-only markup are not needed to appear in them.

faq.question: Where can I see whether my pages appear in AI Overviews?
faq.answer: Use the generative AI performance report in Google Search Console. It shows impressions from AI Overviews and AI Mode, grouped by page, country and device.

faq.question: How often should I review my Google Business Profile?
faq.answer: Once a month, plus before every holiday. Hours and services change more often than most owners expect, and wrong hours cost real customers.
